questions.question: Describe the simple closed economy: its two participants, two markets, and the difference between real and money flows.
questions.expected_answer: Households own all four factors of production — natural resources, labour, capital, entrepreneurship — and supply them to firms through the factor market, earning factor incomes in return: wages, rent, interest and profit. Firms combine the factors into goods and services, which households buy through the goods market; that spending becomes firm revenue and funds the next round of factor payments — the circle spins. Real flows are the physical things — factors travelling to firms, goods travelling to households; money flows are the payments travelling the opposite way — incomes out, spending back. Every real flow has a money flow driving against it.

questions.question: List the three leakages and three injections of the open economy, and explain the 'three doors' pairing.
questions.expected_answer: Leakages: savings, taxes, imports. Injections: investment, government spending, exports. Each leakage exits through the same channel its partner injection re-enters: savings drain out through the financial sector and return as investment when banks lend to firms for capital goods; taxes drain out through the government and return as government spending on salaries, infrastructure, goods and grants; import payments exit across the border and export earnings return across it. Three doors, each with traffic in both directions — and a leakage is not 'bad': the terms describe direction of flow, never virtue.

questions.question: Explain how the balance of leakages and injections determines whether the economy contracts, expands or holds steady, with a street-level sign of each.
questions.expected_answer: When total leakages exceed total injections, less money returns to firms each round: production falls, incomes fall, the circle contracts — quiet tills and shorter shifts on the street. When injections exceed leakages, the circle expands: more spending, more production, more hiring — the good spiral. When they are equal the economy is in equilibrium — the level holds, things feel steady. This is why news about savings behaviour, government budgets, imports and exports matters: every such headline is a drain or a tap, and reading them together estimates whether the water level will rise or fall.
